papers.title: Ratings, Debt, and Deficits: An Exploration
papers.abstract: We look at the effects of debt and primary fiscal balances on sovereign credit ratings through the lens of a simple model. We find that the ratings differ from the implications of the model in three important ways. They give much more weight to debt relative to forecast primary balances. They understate the effects of the difference between the interest rate and the growth rate. They give a very large role to country effects. For the same level of debt and forecast primary balances, they imply extremely different ratings across countries, and imply extremely different levels of debt needed to reach a given rating.

papers.title: Insuring Landlords
papers.abstract: This paper shows that insuring landlords against non-payment risk can improve housing access and upward geographic mobility for fragile tenants. We study Visale, a large-scale publicly funded rent guarantee insurance policy in France, free for eligible tenants and landlords. Using administrative household and claim payout data and quasi-experimental eligibility variation by exact age, we show the guarantee increased access to private-sector rental housing, especially for immigrants, newly formed households, and low-income renters. The scheme eased long-distance mobility toward expensive, high-wage neighborhoods at a moderate fiscal cost per marginal move, though potentially displacing comparable ineligible tenants through higher rents.

papers.title: Optimal Taxation of Indistinguishable Activities
papers.abstract: Optimal tax policy frequently prescribes different tax treatments for activities that are difficult in practice for tax administrators to distinguish, such as expenditures undertaken for business versus personal purposes. We study the optimal design of income tax deductions for such expenditures under the assumption that a common deduction rate must be applied to both forms of the expenditure. The Pareto optimal common deduction turns on the relative compensated spending response for each margin, weighted by the income tax wedge. We also characterize the welfare gain from distinguishing between the two expenditure forms as a harmonic mean of the compensated responses. We illustrate both results with an application to air travel expenses.

papers.title: Selective Admissions in Nursing Homes: Evidence from a Randomized Audit Study
papers.abstract: It has been widely documented that patients in the US who are associated with disadvantaged demographics receive care at lower quality nursing homes. To understand the role that selective admissions may play in contributing to this pattern, we conducted a nationwide audit study of the impact of patient race, payer, and medical condition on responses to about 5,500 availability inquiries sent to about 3,000 nursing homes. We find 10-15% lower availability for Medicaid patients compared to private-pay patients and for patients with Alzheimer’s disease compared to those without; these availability gaps generally increase with nursing home quality. We find no statistically significant evidence of differential availability by race. To quantify the implications of these selective admissions practices, we embed the audit study results in a model of constrained nursing home choice. We estimate that if, counterfactually, Medicaid patients had the same choice sets as their private-pay counterparts, they would attend higher quality nursing homes on average, but the private-Medicaid gap in quality would be reduced by only 5-10%. Our results suggest that supply-side availability differences by payer are widespread, but that they are unlikely to be the primary factor behind the observed gap in quality of nursing homes attended.

papers.title: Homework in Climate Economics: Household Production, Environmental Preferences, and Climate Policy
papers.abstract: Household energy use accounts for approximately one third of U.S. emissions. Guided by a new survey, we develop a quantitative model in which households differ in income and their desire to reduce their emissions. Our analysis of cost-minimizing subsidies for clean equipment, such as electric vehicles and heat pumps, and residential solar yields three insights. First, solar receives the highest subsidy rate and accounts for over one third of abatement, reflecting its complementarities with clean equipment. Second, restricting subsidy eligibility to lower-income households generates only small cost savings. Third, without environmental preferences, household emissions would be over 15 percent higher.
